In the beautiful and forcible Circular addressed by the National to the Subordinate
Division of the Sons of Temperance, which will be found on our first page, occurs this

boring for it, we will learn to love it." How

TUESDAY, April 21—6 P. M.

The tendency of prices in the stock market was downward from the opening this morning. In all the leading railroad stocks there was about the usual activity. In Illinois Central and Cleveland and Pittsburg, however, the transactions were unusually large. The former opened at 131 and closed at 128 per cent and the latter opened SIX and closed at 60 per cent. New York Central Railroad fell 1 per cent; Erie 1; Michigan Southern 1; Cleveland and Chicago, 1. Reading Railroad advanced 1/2 per cent; Chicago and Rock Island, 1/2. Milwaukee, 1/2. The upward movement in Reading is the result of combination of buyers. It opened SIX and closed at 82 1/2 per cent cash. Bear sale of 100 shares made at 79 1/2, seller six months. In Erie the movement this morning was about as before noticed. The books of the company closed for the stock dividend. The addition to the capital by this dividend will be nearly eleven hundred thousand dollars. Just before the closing of the books issue of the old stocks made by the Erie Company for the purpose of raising money on an exchange operation. This stock will draw its ten per cent dividend, and will in time find its way into the market. The company will be able to pay up the loan and withdraw the stock. Its floating debt is now full two millions of dollars, and it must ready increase the face of its loans and stock issues. The Erie Company has within its history funded about half dozen floating debts and it can no longer dispose of such claims in that way. This company is really much worse off at the present moment with its large floating debt than it was three years ago when the stock went down to 20 or 80 per cent. Up to within the past six or eight months, stockholders and the public have been under the belief that cash dividend would be resumed by April this year. The latest, that time has arrived, and the company appears to be further from cash dividend than ever. Instead of ten millions of capital to pay on it, it has upwards of eleven millions with constantly increasing floating debt.

Illinois Central Railroad declined 1/2 per cent; Cleveland and Pittsburg, 1/2. The bears appear to have turned their attention more than usual to Illinois Central Railroad stock. The news from Europe by the steamship Fulton appears to be particularly pleasant to holders of fancy railroad stocks. Upon the strength of the Bank of England advance, attraction was realized in some of invaluable railroad stocks. The favorable prospect for financial affairs generally must have been very encouraging to operators in such stocks. Erie, Cleveland and Toledo, Michigan Southern, and others will change the looks of things and open the eyes of spectators in fancy railroad stocks for a rise. After Christopher Columbus discovered America, and some years later, when the Portuguese Vasco de Gama made out the route to India by the Cape of Good Hope, Spain and Portugal equipped in all haste numerous ships to explore new countries, and for several ages adventurers from these two nations brought back into their respective countries gold from America and precious stones from India. In short time, the immense riches they amassed by this commerce proved the solidity of their speculations. But at the same time that these millionaire grocers sought for useful plants, they did not overlook those which might also flatter the sight. In attempting sketch of this kind, as we

matter is retentive, should excuse them.


The first authentic account we have of the
existence of anything like Post Office in
St. Paul, is in May, 1S49. AT that time it
was kept in a miserable shanty on the (now)
corner of Bench and jackson Streets, by
Henry Jackson. The building is not now
standing, we are told: it was used by Jack
son for trading post, and grog shop The
Post Office part of it was kept in one corner
in desk or cupboard, and as the Post Mast
er was often unable to attend to his duties or
absent, those who wanted letters or papers
would have to look over the diminutive bunch
of greasy, worn, and dirty missives; or the
papers-whch were free to loafers to read
in order to get his mail matter. We believe
Jackson held no commission from Govern
ment, but merely kept his arduous and i'm
portant post by the consent of the people,
We are not indeed informed now as to
whether the group of claims which occupied
the present site of Saint Paul, the metropo-
lis of the North West, was considered of
sufficient Importance to have Post Office
regularly established, or not. We believe

Which Is the MOST successful plan of turning
sinners from the error of their way?
Faithful, fervent prayer? Or speaking of
their faults to others without their knowledge! Often it is the case that the latter
course is pursued instead of the former.
And instead of humbling ourselves in PRAYER
before God, as we should do, we go to our
neighbor and make our complaint, when we
are plainly told in the Bible that if we go to
God and ask in faith, nothing doubting, it
will be done unto us. But alas how often
do we know preachers, and even professors of
religion, yea, some ministers of the Gospel are
not exempt from this practice! Now we
think it becomes us as professors of religion,
to be careful what we say of others, when
they are not present and especially that
which we would not be willing to say to their
faces. Oh the deceitfulness of the human
heart! How often do we hear sinners say,
they do not care of the members of the
church doing this and so, when the preach
er does the very same thing. God grant to
prune the pulpits and laity, and grant that we
may all come out from among the world and
be separated from them. Then will we see
the cause of Christ prosper in our midst.
Brethren, let us all send up our prayers to
God as the voice of one man, to take from
our hearts this practice and engraft in
its stead ceaseless prayer. Oh! What a
change will then be seen and felt amongst
US. Instead of having a complaint against
each other, it would be "glory to God in
the highest, peace and good will to man."
For we cannot see clearly to cast the mote
out of our brother's eye when there is a beam
in our own. When we look around us and
see how far we have departed from true re-
ligion, it is enough to make our hearts trem-
ble within us and cause us to exclaim with
the psalmist, Oh! Lord, how long wilt
thou hide thy face from us. May God
help us in future to place our affections on
things that are more substantial than the
perishing things of earth, and place them
upon things that are heavenly and divine—
things that will not perish with their using
but will shine brighter and brighter, until
the perfect day. God grant that this on-
ly may be, through time and through eter-
nity. GUITA.

The Democratic County Convention of Cass, held at Logansport on the 11th inst. unanimously passed the following resolutions in regard to State policy. It will be seen that the Convention resolved that its proceedings be published in the State Sentinel, but the managers of that paper do not see fit to give them place in its columns.

Why the staunch and reliable Democracy of Cass County is thus ignored by a paper claiming to be the central organ of the party, is no mystery to us. Had their proceedings like the speech of Judge Hugh at Greenfield, been sort of kiss and make up affair between them and the new State Bank, we have no sort of doubt they would have found most welcome place in the columns of the Sentinel.

S. A. Hall, from the committee reported the following resolutions:

Resolved, That the Democracy of Cass County rejoice in the judgment rendered at the ballot-box in favor of Democratic principles redeeming the lower House of Congress from the control of a factional majority, again placing in the departments of the general government in the hands of the National Democracy, and clearly indicating that although falsehood and secret intrigue may temporarily succeed, the sober second thought will always sustain the party that relies upon the intelligence and virtue of the American people.

Resolved, That we have full confidence in the candidacy of James Buchanan, and in his ability to carry the country safely through all difficulties at home and abroad.

Resolved, That we think the interests of the State demand that an extra session of the Legislature should be called at an early day.

Resolved, That we deem it the duty of the State Executive to order an election for Supreme Judges to fill the vacancies occasioned by the resignation of Judge Stewart and Gookins, and that it is the duty of the Democratic State Central Committee to call a Convention at an early day to nominate candidates whether an election is ordered or not.

RESOLVED, That Democratic leaders should be respected and sustained no longer than they sustain in the principles laid down in the National and State platforms of the Democratic party.

Resolved, That in experience teaches that paper money is at war with the rights and interests of the laboring classes—that Banking institutions are monopolies which ought not to be created under the sanction of the Legislature—that the recent failures of banks confirm the warning of General Jackson against them—and that the overthrow of the entire system of paper money banking as now practiced, should be demanded by the people at the hands of their representatives.

Resolved, That the passage of the bill to organize the Bank of the State of Indiana was uncalled for by the people, and an unjustifiable violation of Democratic principles.

Resolved, That we believe an Independent Treasury will work as satisfactorily in State as in National finances, and that it should be established in this State.

Resolved, That we are opposed to the scheme to transfer the Wabash and Erie Canal from the bond-holders to the State—that the consummation of that scheme will fasten upon the people of INDIANA an additional debt of seven millions of dollars, requiring the annual payment of half a million dollars in interest—and that we demand of our representatives an uncompromising opposition to it.

Resolved, That Know-Nothingism is a principle which is utterly opposed to that civil and religious liberty of which we as a people boast—and that the Democratic party is pledged to oppose it whatever phase it may present itself.

The resolutions were unanimously adopted.

On motion of A. M. Gratis,

Convention be published in the Democratic Pharos, and State Sentinel.

-Attempt to send Mrs. Dean out of the country.-
Quite an excitement was created in the upper
part of the city late Tuesday night in consequence of an alleged attempt, on the part of Mr.

and other friends,—to send her out of the coun-

It is said that plans were being laid by Mr.

Europe in direct contravention of her wishes
and desires.

Charles S. Spencer, ESQ., counsel for Dean,
the lucky bridegroom, was called out of bed late
at night to interpose in behalf of Dean, and to
prevent the designs of Mr. Boxer being carried
out. Mr. Edwards, counsel for Mr. Boxer, upon

injunction from Judge Davies preventing any
interference with Mary Ann, by John Dean, the
husband, until the further order of the Court.

New York, Nov. 10, 1857.

Mr. Editor,

You miss it for sending for none, now for I ain't got none. The fax is gone this Fall, & ain't done a stitch of work in many weeks. I suppose war has puzzled my brain, or I'm in a naughty way. Yours til death and we wish her,

Preserved Wicker.

MacAULAY TO BE A PEER. From the latest

English papers, we find that proposition is now being entertained in England, of elevating Thomas Darlington Macaulay to the Peerage, and giving him seat by virtue of the title which is proposed to confer upon him in the House of Lords. This is said to be a measure originating with Lord Palmerston, and we observe that it is heartily seconded by the most powerful British journals. The particular crisis which England's interests are approaching, in her distant possessions in India, seems to be the immediate occasion of this move. It is well known to all who have read the miscellaneous essays of Macaulay, that his papers upon the British rule in India, are among the most masterful of his productions. In his historical sketches of the life and trial of the celebrated Warren Hastings, once Governor General of India, he evinced a knowledge of the workings of the East India Company's financial and moral government which, it is said, no other man in England possessed. Despite the former prosecution of Hastings by the House of Commons, despite the greatest effort of the great Burke, reinforced by the most eloquent defamation that ever fell from the lips of Sheridan, Macaulay did not shrink, alone and single-handed, to lay before the world a very different view of the many inexplicable influences, which, unobserved by the impassioned eyes of Burke and Sheridan, had deprived Hastings of that verdict to which he was fairly entitled, in the judgment of his countrymen. For his intimate knowledge of this now most important matter to England, all eyes have, no doubt, been turned to Macaulay. "A proud era, it must be, to the great historian, notwithstanding the disaster which it portends to his idolized government. A more forcible illustration of the old aphorism, that knowledge is power" could not have been given to the world than this action of an ancient and high-feeling peerage, taking to their midst, not a sinecure or a fill-up, but as their leader and their adviser, a comparatively humble son of genius.
